claims.claim: Storage is the process of holding encoded information over time — the stage between encoding and retrieval. OpenStax Psychology 2e calls storage 'the retention of the encoded information'; the APA Dictionary of Psychology defines storage as the state of an item that is retained in memory, after encoding and before retrieval; the Noba Project defines storage as maintaining information over time.

The three-store account of memory — sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory — was proposed by Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968); their model treats memory like an information-processing system, and the stores are models of how memory behaves, not literal places in the brain.

Sensory memory holds raw information from the senses very briefly. Iconic memory (visual sensory memory) holds an image for less than a second; echoic memory (auditory sensory memory) retains sounds for about 2-3 seconds after the stimulus ends. OpenStax describes sensory memory overall as very brief storage, up to a couple of seconds.

Short-term memory holds a limited amount of material for a short time: OpenStax says storage lasts 15 to 30 seconds; the APA Dictionary says recall of a limited amount of material occurs after a period of about 10 to 30 seconds. Widely cited capacity figures include George Miller's (1956) 'magic number' of 7 plus or minus 2 items and Nelson Cowan's (2010) more recent estimate of 4 plus or minus 1 for working memory capacity.

Working memory, refined in the 1974 model of Baddeley and Hitch, extends short-term memory: it is the system that briefly retains information in a highly accessible state and actively manipulates it, rather than merely holding it.

Long-term memory is a relatively permanent information storage system that enables retention, retrieval, and use of skills and knowledge hours, weeks, or even years after learning; its storage capacity is believed to be effectively unlimited.

Consolidation is the process by which a memory becomes stable and permanent following a learning experience (APA Dictionary). OpenStax adds the timescale: once information reaches long-term memory it is consolidated at the synaptic level over a few hours and into the memory system over weeks or longer. Rehearsal — active (repetition) or elaborative (linking to existing knowledge) — moves information from short-term toward long-term storage.

Memory involves networks, not a single file: long-term memories are organized in associative (semantic) networks in which activating one concept spreads to linked concepts (Collins & Loftus, 1975, as reported by OpenStax), and a memory trace is the physical change in the nervous system that represents an experience.

Storage is not a vault of exact copies: memory traces are not perfect packets of information, are not like video or audio recordings, and remembering is reconstructive (we rebuild the past with the aid of traces and current beliefs), not reproductive (Noba Project).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Capacity and duration figures for short-term/working memory differ across sources and researchers.
positions: Miller (1956): short-term capacity about 7 plus or minus 2 items (OpenStax).
Cowan (2010): working memory capacity closer to 4 plus or minus 1 (OpenStax).
Duration: OpenStax says 15 to 30 seconds; APA Dictionary says about 10 to 30 seconds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states these as widely cited estimates, each attributed to its named researcher or source, and avoids treating any figure as exact. The lesson's wording ('roughly', 'about', 'believed to be') reflects the estimates' status.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sensory memory duration is described at different levels of specificity.
positions: OpenStax: sensory memory is very brief storage, up to a couple of seconds.
APA Dictionary: iconic memory holds an image for less than a second; echoic memory retains sounds for about 2-3 seconds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the more specific APA per-sense figures (iconic less than a second; echoic about 2-3 seconds) and notes the overall brevity of sensory memory, citing both sources.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No machine-generated draft claims were retained; the generated draft (public/content/phase-4/lessons.json entry) was treated as editorial intent only and its boilerplate wording was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: All capacity/duration numbers are attributed to named researchers or sources (Miller 1956; Cowan 2010; OpenStax 15-30 s; APA iconic <1 s; echoic 2-3 s) — no unattributed or invented figures.
The three stores are consistently framed as models (Atkinson-Shiffrin 1968; Baddeley-Hitch 1974), never as literal brain locations.
Consolidation is described as a gradual process (hours at the synaptic level; weeks or longer into the memory system, per OpenStax), not an instantaneous transfer.
The honest framing (storage is not a vault; remembering is reconstructive) is carried through the lesson, questions, and takeaway.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via Internet Archive snapshot (web.archive.org, 2026 capture). Supports: memory as the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information; storage as the retention of the encoded information; Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) three-stage model (sensory, short-term, long-term memory); sensory memory as very brief storage up to a couple of seconds; short-term memory lasting 15 to 30 seconds; Miller's (1956) 7 plus or minus 2 and Cowan's (2010) 4 plus or minus 1 capacity estimates; Peterson and Peterson (1959) decay findings; Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) working memory model; consolidation at the synaptic level (a few hours) and into the memory system (weeks or longer); long-term memory as continuous storage with capacity believed unlimited; active and elaborative rehearsal; semantic (associative) networks (Collins & Loftus, 1975). Facts synthesized in original wording.
